deep.reconstruction:
WHAT THE PAGE IS. Folio 13v is one sheet of a large ruled table, numbered (13) on the previous page and (14) on the next. Each page has 24 columns headed by consecutive primes. Here they run 509, 521, 523, 541, 547, 557, 563, 569, 571, 577, 587, 593, 599, 601, 607, 613, 617, 619, 631, 641, 643, 647, 653, 659. The previous page covers 367–503 and the next 661–827, so the column primes evidently run through all primes below 1000. Thick rules mark every 6 columns. The rows are primes, grouped in blocks. Only the bottom block is labelled: 953, 971, 977, 983, 991, 997. The prime 967 has no label, although a wider gap sits between 953 and 971. All upper blocks are empty, as are rows 953 and 971. Only rows 977, 983, 991 and 997 carry entries. Same-row entries in adjacent columns are joined by short horizontal strokes, and same-column entries in vertically adjacent filled rows by vertical strokes. This is a purely visual device that produces the 'molecule' figures.

MEANING OF A CIRCLE (my verification). A circle in row q, column p means that p is a quadratic residue mod q, i.e. the Legendre symbol (p/q) = +1. I checked this independently by quadratic reciprocity (Jacobi-style reduction) for every cell of the four filled rows. Below, a dash or a semicolon separates groups of circles joined by strokes.

Row 977 (977 ≡ 1 mod 8, so (p/977) = (977 mod p / p)). Residues: 521, 523, 541, 557, 571, 577, 601, 607, 619, 647, 653, 659. The drawing shows 521–523–541; 557; 571–577; 601–607; 619; 647–653–659. This is an exact match. Sample cases:
- 977 − 521 = 456 = 8·3·19, and (2/521)(3/521)(19/521) = (+1)(−1)(−1) = +1.
- 977 − 509 = 468 = 4·9·13, and (13/509) = (509/13) = (2/13) = −1, so 509 is not a residue.

Row 991 (991 ≡ 3 mod 4, so (p/991) = ±(991/p) according to p mod 4). Residues: 521, 557, 577, 601, 607, 619, 641, 643, 659. The drawing shows 521; 557; 577; 601–607; 619; 641–643; 659. This is an exact match. Sample cases:
- (607/991) = −(991/607) = −(384/607) = −(3/607) = +1.
- (643/991) = −(348/643) = −(3/643)(29/643) = +1.

Row 997 (997 ≡ 5 mod 8). Residues: 509, 521, 563, 569, 577, 593, 607, 619, 631, 641, 647, 653. The drawing shows 509–521; 563–569; 577; 593; 607; 619–631–641; 647–653. This is an exact match. Sample case: (509/997) = (488/509) = (8/509)(61/509) = (−1)(−1) = +1.

Row 983 (983 ≡ 7 mod 8). The correct residues are 521, 523, 547, 557, 563, 571, 577, 587, 613, 617, 619, 631. The drawing, as I read it, shows 523; 547–557–563; 571–577–587; 613–617–619–631–641; 653. Apart from 521, 641 and 653, all agree. Discrepancies:
- (521/983) = (462/521) = (2)(3)(7)(11 / 521) = (+1)(−1)(−1)(+1) = +1, yet no circle appears.
- (641/983) = (342/641) = (19/641) = (14/19) = −1, yet a circle appears.
- (653/983) = (330/653) = (2)(3)(5)(11 / 653) = (−1)(−1)(−1)(+1) = −1, yet a circle appears.

The vertical strokes are consistent with these readings. For example, 523 at row 977 connects down to 983. Column 619 has circles in all four rows 977–997. Column 641 links rows 983–991–997.

PURPOSE. This is an extension of the residue table, Tabula II of Disquisitiones Arithmeticae Art. 99, which only treats small primes as residues against moduli up to 503. Here it becomes a complete square table of quadratic characters between primes below 1000. By reciprocity, each entry (p/q) with p, q odd is equivalent to (q/p) up to the sign (−1)^((p−1)(q−1)/4). The rows appear to have been filled from the bottom (largest moduli 997, 991, 983, 977 first), with 971 and 953 not yet begun on this or the neighbouring pages. Such a table serves Gauss's computational number theory: residue characters of forms, genera, factoring tests, and the empirical control of reciprocity. Nothing on the page is derived; it is a data table.
errors: Row 983, column 521: 521 is a quadratic residue of 983 ((521/983) = +1), but no circle appears (apparent omission).
Row 983, column 641: a circle appears, but (641/983) = (19/641) = (14/19) = −1 (apparent false entry).
Row 983, column 653: a circle appears under 653 (linked to the 977 chain), but (653/983) = (2/653)(3/653)(5/653)(11/653) = −1 (apparent false entry).
These three row-983 discrepancies depend on my reading of circle positions. Rows 977, 991 and 997 match the true residue sets exactly, which suggests the column alignment is read correctly.

Not an error, but notable: row 967 is not labelled although 967 is prime; rows 953 and 971 are unfilled even though they contain residues (e.g. (509/953) = −1 but others are +1), so the table is incomplete, not empty by design.

results.what: Table of quadratic residue characters (p/q) for primes p in 509..659 against moduli q = 977, 983, 991, 997, part of a full table for primes below 1000
results.modern_name: Table of Legendre symbols / quadratic residue table
results.usually_credited_to: Residue tables go back to Gauss's Disquisitiones (1801, Tabula II); larger tables were compiled by 19th-century computers (e.g. Jacobi's Canon Arithmeticus 1839 gives indices from which residues follow)

results.what: Graphical convention linking adjacent residue marks horizontally and vertically

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine computational table of quadratic residues, an extension of the kind Gauss published in Disquisitiones Art. 99 (Tabula II). It is well known that he computed such tables extensively. The only points of interest are the scale (all primes below 1000), the bottom-up filling order, and a few apparent slips in row 983.
